In our view, the decision was puzzling. It reminds us of someone standing in a room with a fire alarm blaring and smoke pouring under the door, yet insisting on more evidence before calling the fire department. Thursday's economic data only reinforced our conviction that the Fed should have raised rates by 25bps on Wednesday.

Consumer spending and business investment are driving the US economic boom. Federal government spending is too, rising 15.8% last quarter.

MarketWatch: Almost double the amount of large-capitalization U.S. stocks moved in the opposite direction to the wider market this year than during the peak of the dot-com crash, according to an asset management firm.

According to quant strategist Kyle Schmidt of NISA Investment Advisers, 27% of large U.S. stocks had negative realized beta in the six months ended Sept. 30, versus a long-run average of 1.3% and a rate of 14% in 2020, when technology stocks crashed.

That's the highest since at least 1990. "This dislocation is extreme in both breadth and duration and has significant implications for portfolio and risk management," Schmidt said.

"We see the market as clearly splitting along the dimension of AI and most everything else," he added.

Per FactSet’s John Butters, the Mag 7 are now reporting lower Q3 earnings growth than the other 493: 22.6% vs. 32.6%. If that holds through the end of earnings season, it’s the first time since Q4 2022. On Sep 30 the expectation was the reverse, at 33.6% vs. 27.8%.

But note it’s largely a function of big GAAP charges at two companies (FactSet uses GAAP EPS for Alphabet, Amazon and Meta):
▪ Meta: −41% vs. estimate, with a $9.89B litigation charge in the quarter
▪ Alphabet: −30% vs. estimate, with $8.7B of net losses on equity securities
▪ Amazon: a tough comparison, since year-ago EPS included $9.5B in pre-tax gains on its Anthropic stake

Microsoft and Tesla both beat, and Apple reports next week while NVIDIA doesn’t report until Nov 17.

The part that isn’t accounting: analysts also expect the Mag 7 to trail in Q4 (22.6% vs. 30.8%), and that gap has widened since Sep 30 (23.6% vs. 28.3%). 

The 493 are being lifted by Energy, where Q4 estimates rose 20.3% in October.

tweets.text:
Did human evolution make the Industrial Revolution inevitable?

The International HapMap Project showed that evolution accelerated roughly a hundredfold starting about 10,000 years ago.

More recent data has clarified exactly what traits have been under selection. David Reich and his collaborators analyzed the genomes of 15,836 individuals from West Eurasia who lived over the past 18,000 years.

Their paper in Nature showed that certain genetic variants that in the modern age were linked to higher intelligence, more years of schooling, and greater income had become more widespread in humans. Conversely, genetic variants that were more prevalent in smokers and those who suffered from certain mental disorders had become less common. 

Consistent with the genetic data, economic historian Gregory Clark documented that members of skilled professions in medieval England had twice as many surviving children as unskilled workers. Indeed, the fledgling middle class of the time had even more surviving children than the aristocracy, who were often out fighting wars. As a result, craftsmen’s wages declined by a third relative to laborers between 1200 and 1800, implying that the supply of skilled labor grew more quickly than the supply of unskilled workers. 

The stunning implication of Clark’s work was that the timing of the Industrial Revolution was a question of “when, not if.”

Full report (ungated): https://t.co/8xxXkwiP9f
